title: The Quote Is the Easy Part: U.S. Trucking Insurance Renewals, Nuclear Verdicts and the Data Underwriters Want for Jan. 1, 2027
summary: U.S. trucking auto liability heads into Jan. 1, 2027 renewals under severity and verdict pressure. What underwriters ask for and how to set retentions.
body_markdown:
The indication lands in the second week of November. A 140-truck regional carrier with a clean year on paper sees its primary auto liability up by a third, and the $5 million excess layer above it repriced again. The underwriter's follow-up email is short. Send camera event counts and coaching closure rates for the last 12 months, by driver. Send continuous MVR monitoring results, not the annual pulls. Send a narrative on the three open bodily injury claims, with dates of first notice. The safety director knows the coaching happened. She cannot prove when, for whom, or what followed, because the answers live in a camera portal, a spreadsheet and a few hundred emails.


The scenario is illustrative. The pattern is not. Heading into Jan. 1, 2027, the renewal is less a price negotiation than an evidence review.


## What the market data actually says


The cost curve has separated from the crash curve. A May 19, 2026 trucking research institute report on insurance costs found liability premiums rose 18.6% from 2021 to 2024, to 10.2 cents per mile, outpacing consumer inflation by 5.4 percentage points. Over the same period, heavy-duty truck-involved crash rates fell 2.6% industry-wide. Among respondents, per-mile liability losses rose an average of 33.1%. Fewer crashes, far more expensive claims. The same report found per-mile premium for the $5 million to $10 million layer rose 34% to 1.58 cents, and the $10 million to $15 million layer rose 45% to 1.05 cents.


Forward-looking indicators do not show relief. An October 1, 2026 broker market outlook projects 2027 commercial auto rate increases of 5% to 15% for well-managed middle-market accounts, and 10% to 20% for high-hazard or challenged classes, while property and workers' compensation soften. An industry research institute and actuarial forecast, as reported in trade press on Nov. 3, 2026, puts the 2026 U.S. commercial auto net combined ratio at 100.9 and expects the line to stay above 100 through 2028. In the same coverage, a transportation wholesale broker said trucking insurers were citing an underlying trend requirement of about 8.5% to 9%, with the best accounts still seeing flat to 5% renewals and multiple options, and weaker accounts facing 30% to 40% increases, fewer markets or non-renewal.


The average does not matter. Your position in the distribution does.


## Social inflation, tort reform and litigation funding: what changed in 2025 and 2026


Underwriters price venue as much as fleet, and state reform has moved unevenly.


**Georgia.** SB 68, signed April 21, 2025, lets parties demand bifurcation of fault and damages in most injury and wrongful death trials, restricts "anchoring" arguments for noneconomic damages, allows juries to see what was actually paid for medical care rather than only the billed amount, makes letters of protection discoverable, and lifts the bar on seatbelt evidence. The companion SB 69 required litigation financiers to register with the state starting Jan. 1, 2026.


**Louisiana.** Changes effective Jan. 1, 2026, as reported by trucking trade press in December 2025, moved the state from pure to modified comparative fault (51% or more at fault recovers nothing), let juries see the amounts insurers actually paid for medical care rather than billed charges, and required commercial vehicle insurers to offer a discount at issue or renewal to policyholders who show dash cams or telematics installed and working.


**New York.** Part EE of Chapter 58 of the Laws of 2026, signed May 26, 2026, applies to motor vehicle actions commenced on or after that date, according to a New York Department of Financial Services circular letter. It repeals the 90/180-day serious injury category, requires the trier of fact to decide fault before serious injury, bars recovery where the claimant's fault exceeds the defendants' combined fault, and caps noneconomic damages at $100,000 for certain at-fault claimants who were uninsured, convicted of impaired driving, or committing a felony. Death cases are excluded.


**Litigation funding.** A 2026 insurance industry issues brief released Oct. 20 counts more than 20 states regulating third-party litigation funding. The 2026 class includes Ohio's HB 105, effective Oct. 6, 2026, which requires commercial funding agreements to be produced to parties and to insurers with a potential duty to defend without a discovery request; North Carolina's HB 315, signed June 22, 2026, an outright ban with civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation; and new laws in Tennessee, Mississippi and Utah.


**Federal.** Nothing has been enacted. The FAIR Trucking Act (H.R. 5268), introduced Sept. 10, 2025 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, would give federal courts original jurisdiction over interstate truck crash cases above $5 million with diverse parties. The Litigation Funding Transparency Act of 2026 (S. 3826), introduced Feb. 11, 2026, has not left Senate Judiciary. A bill to tax litigation funder proceeds (H.R. 3512) drew supportive comments from the Treasury Secretary at a Sept. 15, 2026 House hearing, per trade press, but it has not been enacted.


Reform helps at the margin. A trucking specialist broker quoted in a Nov. 9, 2026 insurance trade article described Florida's reforms as "holding the tide" rather than lowering rates. Do not budget a reduction because your state passed a bill, but do show mileage by state, because underwriters now price New York, Georgia and Louisiana exposure differently.


## What underwriters ask for now, and what they are really testing


**Camera and telematics data.** "Installed" earns little. The May 2026 research found road-facing and driver-facing cameras did not show a statistically significant correlation with lower per-mile liability losses, likely because nearly every respondent had road-facing cameras and coaching practices for driver-facing cameras vary widely. Six crash avoidance technologies did correlate with lower losses, led by forward collision warning. So the camera question is really a coaching question: event volume per driver, time from event to coaching, repeat rates, and what your written policy says happens on the third repeat.


**Driver files.** Expect questions about continuous license monitoring, not just the annual review. Underwriters want to know how fast you would learn that a driver lost a license between annual pulls.


**Claims handling.** Late first notice is now an underwriting flag. A wholesale broker in the Nov. 3 coverage urged same-day reporting even with incomplete facts, because insurers watch whether operators try to manage incidents themselves first. Your submission should show reported date versus loss date for every claim.


**Financial stress.** Underwriters are reading maintenance spend, equipment age and driver turnover as leading indicators of loss. With the same research group's July 2026 operating cost report putting average cost at a record $2.336 per mile in 2025, deferred maintenance is the first thing they look for.


## Retentions, captives and the shape of the tower


The highest-leverage renewal decision is rarely the rate. It is how much risk you keep and where the layers attach.


In the May 2026 report, fleets with 100 or fewer trucks spent a median 4.8% of revenue on liability premium in 2024. Fleets of 101 to 1,000 trucks that did not self-insure spent a median 4.7%, while self-insured fleets of that size spent 2.3%, most with retentions between $250,000 and $1 million. All respondents with 501 to 1,000 trucks self-insured, at a median $1 million. Across 2021 to 2024, combined cost of risk improved as fleets retained more of the initial layer, up to about 10% of it. Above 10%, results depended heavily on the individual fleet, because per-mile losses ran markedly higher in those groups.


Three tradeoffs follow.


**Retention.** A larger retention buys premium relief and, importantly, control. The report notes a common plaintiff tactic of demanding a settlement right at a layer's attachment point, which gives that insurer an incentive to settle high to remove its own risk; a self-insured layer blunts it. The cost is volatility and liquidity. A $500,000 retention means nothing if one bad quarter of claims hits cash you never reserved.


**Limits.** Many fleets trimmed total limits during the 2010s to reduce policy-limits settlements, and the same report found 96.2% of state court motor vehicle tort cases settled. But a visible gap between limits and enterprise value can push a plaintiff to try the catastrophic case. Set limits against your balance sheet and venue mix, not last year's tower.


**Captives and groups.** Member-owned group captives let strong operators keep underwriting profit, at the price of capital, multi-year commitment, shared loss experience and data good enough to be priced accurately. If you beat the market and can document why, it is a serious option. If you cannot, it is a capital call waiting to happen.


## Asset, broker and hybrid: different exposures, different files


**Asset carriers** own the primary auto exposure and the full conversation above. The federal minimum for general freight remains $750,000, below what many shippers and brokers require, so the question is how your tower fits the limits customers demand.


**Brokers** are now priced on contingent auto liability with Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II (May 14, 2026) in the background, and the Oct. 1 outlook names that decision as widening broker exposure. Read the policy wording, not the summary: whether it responds to negligent selection allegations, whether defense costs erode limits, and whether carrier-selection warranties void coverage if your team skips a step. Your evidence is selection records, not camera data.


**Hybrids** face both submissions at once, and the risk is that they blur. If an underwriter cannot tell which loads moved on your authority with your drivers and which you brokered, they will price the worse of the two. Keep records, contracts and communications separable, and report revenue and miles by mode on demand.


## What to do in the next six weeks


1.


Pull your own loss runs and reconcile them to your claims records before the underwriter does. Close stale reserves where you can.


2.


Produce coaching evidence: events, closure time and repeat rate by driver for 12 months.


3.


Document license monitoring frequency and what triggers an out-of-service status.


4.


Model two or three retention options against a bad-year loss scenario and confirm the cash is there.


5.


For brokers and hybrids, export carrier selection records showing what was checked at tender time and who approved overrides.


## Turning operations into evidence


No two freight operations carry the same risk. Lanes, venues, customers, driver pools and asset-to-brokered mix all differ, which is why underwriters price individually and why a generic safety letter moves nothing. The shops that renew well have encoded their own risk policy into the system they run every day: driver statuses that block dispatch when a license check fails, required documents before a load can move, claims workflows that time-stamp first notice and every reserve change, permissions that control who can override a rule and require a reason, and visibility into miles by state and mode without a spreadsheet. When the underwriter's email arrives, the answer is a report, not a project.


## FAQ


### How much will U.S. trucking auto liability insurance rise at Jan. 1, 2027 renewals?


Most forecasts point to continued increases, with an October 2026 broker outlook projecting 5% to 15% for well-managed middle-market commercial auto accounts and 10% to 20% for challenged classes. Individual trucking renewals vary widely, from flat for the best accounts to 30% to 40% for weaker ones, according to Nov. 3, 2026 trade coverage.


### Why are premiums rising when truck crash rates are falling?


Claim severity, not frequency, is driving cost. A May 2026 trucking research report found crash rates fell 2.6% from 2021 to 2024 while per-mile liability losses among respondents rose 33.1%, with excess layers repricing fastest.


### Do dash cams lower trucking insurance premiums?


Cameras alone rarely move price, because underwriters look at what you do with the footage. The same research found no statistically significant link between cameras and lower losses, though Louisiana now requires commercial vehicle insurers to offer a discount when dash cams or telematics are installed and working.


### Should a mid-size fleet raise its self-insured retention?


Possibly, if it has the cash reserves and claims capability to absorb a bad year. The May 2026 research found combined cost of risk improved as fleets retained up to about 10% of their initial layer, with results above that level depending heavily on the individual fleet.


### Is there a federal law limiting nuclear verdicts against trucking companies?


No, there is no enacted federal limit. The FAIR Trucking Act (H.R. 5268), introduced in September 2025, would move qualifying interstate truck crash cases above $5 million into federal court, but it has not become law.
